chain.g: a small swelling, bump, or protuberance; a boil, pimple, tubercle

ety.text: To international scientific vocabulary from New Latin tūberculōsis, from Latin tūberculum (diminutive of tūber (“lump”)) + Latin -ōsis (“diseased condition”); by surface analysis, tubercul(um) + -osis; named for the encapsulated colonies of Mycobacterium tuberculosis within the lungs in pulmonary tuberculosis, which can look like small tubers (tubercles) on gross pathology.

senses.d: An infectious disease of humans and animals caused by a species of mycobacterium, usually Mycobacterium tuberculosis, mainly infecting the lungs where it causes tubercles characterized by the expectoration of mucus and sputum, fever, weight loss, and chest pain, and transmitted through inhalation or ingestion of bacteria.
ex: With smallpox gone, tuberculosis is today the deadliest infectious disease on the planet.

ety.text: From Scientific Latin tuberculosis, from tubercŭlum (“tiny tumor”) and + -osis.

chain.g: long trumpet over 1 meter in length, especially a war-trumpet

ety.text: From Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”), related to tuba (“long trumpet; war-trumpet”), of obscure ultimate origin, but possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-pipe”); see there. Doublet of tubus.

senses.d: Anything that is hollow and cylindrical in shape.
An approximately cylindrical container, usually with a crimped end and a screw top, used to contain and dispense semiliquid substances.
ex: A tube of toothpaste.

senses.d: The London Underground railway system, originally referred to the lower level lines that ran in tubular tunnels as opposed to the higher ones which ran in rectangular section tunnels. (Often the tube.)
ex: I took the tube to Waterloo and walked the rest of the way.
He took the tube to Westminster and disappeared.

senses.d: One of the tubular tunnels of the London Underground.
A tin can containing beer.
ex: Beer is also available from bottleshops (or bottle-o's) in cases (or 'slabs') of 24-36 cans (‘tinnies' or ‘tubes') or bottles (‘stubbies') of 375ml each.
It's alright to cop a warm tube of Fosters and a cold pie 'n' peas when you're dated by one of the locals[.]

senses.d: A wave which pitches forward when breaking, creating a hollow space inside.
ex: It seemed like Butch was invincible, like he could do nothing wrong, coming through one unbelievable tube after another.

senses.d: A television. Compare cathode ray tube and picture tube.
ex: I sit around and watch the tube, but nothing's on. I change the channels for an hour or two.

senses.d: An idiot.
ex: 'Don't be a bloody tube, Jack,' she told me. (I always loved it when she used Scottish terms of abuse in that English accent of hers.)
I'm a tube? Who got done for speeding? Who got lifted for bloody assault?

senses.d: To supply with, or enclose in, a tube.
ex: She tubes lipstick in the cosmetics factory.

senses.d: To ride an inner tube.
ex: They tubed down the Colorado River.

senses.d: To intubate.
ex: The patient was tubed.

ety.text: From Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”).

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese, borrowed from the same Andalusian Arabic source as Spanish biznaga (“toothpickweed”) passed from Latin pastināca (“parsnip”).

Inherited from Middle French tuyau, from Old French tuel, tuial, tudel (“tube, pipe”), from Frankish *thūta (“pipe”), from Proto-Germanic *þeutǭ (“pipe, channel, flow”), from *þeutaną (“to howl, roar, resound”), from Proto-Indo-European *tu-, *tutu- (“bird-cry, shriek”).
Borrowed from Mozarabic *qannût, from Vulgar Latin *cannūtus (“resembling sugarcane”), from Latin canna (“cane”).
From Latin latus (“wide, extensive”); or from Italian latta (“tin can”).
From Middle English tubbe, tobbe, from Middle Dutch tubbe or Middle Low German tubbe, tobbe, further etymology unknown. Considered to be unrelated to tube.

senses.d: A flat-bottomed vessel, of width similar to or greater than its height, used for storing or packing things, or for washing things in.
ex: He bought a tub of lard to roast the potatoes in.

senses.d: The contents or capacity of such a vessel.
ex: She added a tub of margarine to the stew.

senses.d: A bathtub.
A slow-moving craft.
Any structure shaped like a tub, such as a certain old form of pulpit, a short broad boat, etc.
ex: All being took up and busied, some in pulpits and some in tubs, in the grand work of preaching and holding forth.

senses.d: A small cask.
ex: a tub of gin

senses.d: Any of various historically designated quantities of goods to be sold by the tub (butter, oysters, etc).
A box or bucket in which coal or ore is sent up a shaft.
A sweating in a tub; a tub fast.
ex:
tubs and baths; bring down rose-cheeked youth
To the tub-fast and the diet

senses.d: A corpulent or obese person.
To plant, set, or store in a tub.
ex: to tub a plant

senses.d: To bathe in a tub.

Don't we all "tub" in England?
